protocol.instrument_name: Queensland Community Pharmacy Travel Health - Clinical Practice Guideline
protocol.legal_basis: Not stated in this document; issued by Queensland Health as a Queensland Community Pharmacy clinical practice guideline for a prescribing service (page 1).
protocol.supervision_model: Document's own terminology: pharmacists are advised to 'exercise professional discretion and judgement' and to decide 'in consultation with the patient and/or their parent/caregiver'; pharmacists must prescribe according to 'the specified sections of the current online version of the Therapeutic Guidelines'. No 'collaborative'/'autonomous' label is printed.
protocol.scope_summary: Clinical practice guideline for pharmacist-led pre-travel health consultations in Queensland community pharmacies: comprehensive pre-travel risk assessment (Table 1), high-risk traveller referral, vaccination and International Certificate of Vaccination, rabies pre-exposure prophylaxis, travellers' diarrhoea, malaria chemoprophylaxis and stand-by treatment, altitude illness, VTE, medical kits, travelling with medications, traveller education and post-travel advice. Service restricted to patients aged 2 years or over (diarrhoea) and 8 years or over (Malaria, Altitude sickness). No drug strength or dose is printed anywhere; pharmacotherapy is delegated to the specified sections of the current online Therapeutic Guidelines.

inclusion.text: Service restricted to patients aged 2 years or over (diarrhoea)
Service restricted to patients aged 8 years or over (Malaria, Altitude sickness)

exclusion.text: children aged ≤8 years travelling to areas of altitude above 2,500 m or who require malaria prophylaxis or stand-by treatment
travellers visiting areas where malaria is endemic for longer than 8 weeks
pregnant travellers or travellers planning to become pregnant while travelling
travellers that require a vaccination that is not able to be administered in the community pharmacy setting or contraindicated
immunocompromised travellers, as per the CDC Yellow Book 2026: immunocompromised travellers
travellers with conditions that may be worsened by air travel or high altitudes by hypoxaemia

travellers with chronic diseases or medical conditions that are not well controlled or are severe (e.g., renal, liver, cardiovascular, respiratory and pulmonary diseases, diabetes, epilepsy, autoimmune and rheumatologic diseases, psychiatric illness, mental health conditions)
recent surgery, trauma or injury (consult individual airlines and travel insurers for specific rules regarding to fitness to fly, including post-operatively)
moderate or high risk of VTE
official medical clearance to travel/fitness to fly certification is needed
travellers whose regular medication(s) are not permitted in the planned destination

travellers undertaking high risk activities including: travel in areas of very high or extreme altitude (>3,500 m); moderate to high-risk ascents in high/very high-altitude areas; extreme sports, mountaineering or activities in remote locations; international aid work or military posting.
people travelling for medical treatment overseas e.g., dental treatment, cosmetic surgery, overseas-based clinical trials
travellers returning (or arriving) with post-travel issues/symptoms (immediate referral is required if malaria is suspected).

exclusion_exceptions.text: Ineligibility for treatment as part of a prescribing service does not preclude a patient from accessing services provided as part of usual pharmacy care.

diagnosis_pathways.name: Travel health - pre-travel consultation, condition-specific management and post-travel advice

steps.description: Refer when: Refer the patient to an appropriate healthcare provider in the following situations: children aged ≤8 years travelling to areas of altitude above 2,500 m or who require malaria prophylaxis or stand-by treatment; travellers visiting areas where malaria is endemic for longer than 8 weeks; pregnant travellers or travellers planning to become pregnant while travelling; travellers that require a vaccination that is not able to be administered in the community pharmacy setting or contraindicated; immunocompromised travellers, as per the CDC Yellow Book 2026: immunocompromised travellers; travellers with conditions that may be worsened by air travel or high altitudes by hypoxaemia; travellers with chronic diseases or medical conditions that are not well controlled or are severe (e.g., renal, liver, cardiovascular, respiratory and pulmonary diseases, diabetes, epilepsy, autoimmune and rheumatologic diseases, psychiatric illness, mental health conditions); recent surgery, trauma or injury (consult individual airlines and travel insurers for specific rules regarding to fitness to fly, including post-operatively); moderate or high risk of VTE; official medical clearance to travel/fitness to fly certification is needed; travellers whose regular medication(s) are not permitted in the planned destination; travellers undertaking high risk activities including: travel in areas of very high or extreme altitude (>3,500 m), moderate to high-risk ascents in high/very high-altitude areas, extreme sports, mountaineering or activities in remote locations, international aid work or military posting; people travelling for medical treatment overseas e.g., dental treatment, cosmetic surgery, overseas-based clinical trials; travellers returning (or arriving) with post-travel issues/symptoms (immediate referral is required if malaria is suspected). Each situation is captured individually as RF-1 to RF-18 and as eligibility exclusions EXC-1 to EXC-14. Page 3 note: 'While conducting the pre-travel health consultation, pharmacists should be aware of the requirements for referral to other healthcare providers as these may become apparent at various stages throughout the consultation.'

gates.criterion: No 'Refer when' criterion present

steps.description: Key points: The primary purpose of the pre-travel health consultation is to minimise the traveller’s risk of injury and illness by providing advice, education, vaccinations, medicines and/or medical kits tailored to each individual’s personal and itinerary risks (1-4). Pre-travel consultations should be conducted as far in advance of departure as possible (ideally 6-8 weeks) to allow sufficient time for vaccination courses to be undertaken and commencement of malaria chemoprophylaxis if required (2, 5). Practitioners providing travel medicine services should have a working knowledge (and know how to access current and accurate information) of the global epidemiology of infectious and non-infectious diseases, health risks, trends in drug-resistant infections, and destination-specific regulations regarding immunisation and the importation and use of medications (1, 2, 4).

Patient history and assessment / Pre-travel risk assessment: Travel health consultations should be tailored to the needs of each patient. An effective pre-travel consultation should include a comprehensive pre-travel risk assessment based on the traveller's medical history, travel history, itinerary and travel details, as per Table 1 (3). Obtain sufficient information from the patient to assess the safety and appropriateness of any recommendations and medicines. Table 1. Components of a comprehensive pre-travel risk assessment - Patient history: age; pregnancy (current or planned) and lactation status (if applicable); medical history including past and current conditions: conditions that influence susceptibility/severity of infections or immunocompromise e.g., splenectomy, steroid therapy, active or recent cancer; conditions that may cause acute illness or require emergency treatment while overseas e.g., asthma, diabetes, severe allergies and past allergic reactions; conditions increasing susceptibility to hypoxia e.g., cardiorespiratory disease, severe anaemia; immunocompromise; mental illness and current psychological state; chronic conditions e.g., rheumatologic disorders; colostomy or ileostomy; disability or impairment; conditions that may impact on effectiveness or safety of malarial prophylaxis e.g. previous malaria, central nervous system disease or cardiac conditions; ongoing hormone treatment e.g., estrogen therapy, oral contraceptive pill, menopausal hormone therapy; thrombophilic conditions; history of venous thromboembolism (VTE); recent surgery or injury (individual airlines and travel insurers have rules regarding fitness to fly post-operatively; these should be reviewed on a case-by-case basis); recent cardiopulmonary and/or cerebrovascular event.

provenance.section_heading: Table 1. Components of a comprehensive pre-travel risk assessment(1-4)

steps.description: Table 1 (continued from page 3): Patient history - current treatments (including prescribed medicines, vitamins, herbs, other supplements, and over-the-counter medicines), particularly medications that may be prohibited in other countries, require supporting documentation, or require advice to be taken safely across time zones; allergies/adverse drug reactions, including allergies to vaccines; alcohol and drug history (considering destination regulations); smoking status; immunisation history (routine and travel vaccinations); obesity (BMI). Travel history: previous travel experience, including experience with chemoprophylaxis for malaria; experience at high altitudes (if applicable to destination); VTE prophylaxis; experience with travel-related and other relevant illnesses. Itinerary and travel details: countries and regions in itinerary, considering remoteness, access and quality of medical facilities, hygiene, epidemiology of infectious diseases, season and likely weather conditions; duration of total trip and duration of stay in each area; reason for travel e.g., leisure, 'health tourism', international development or aid work; planned activities e.g., snow sports, scuba diving, moped/vehicle use, disaster relief, long distance walking or cycling; risk of acquiring sexually transmitted infections (STIs)/sexual history; travel style, considering mode of transport and travel times e.g., cruise ships, long-haul flights, backpacking, guided tours, traveller risk tolerance, accommodation type.

provenance.section_heading: Table 1. Components of a comprehensive pre-travel risk assessment(1-4)

steps.description: High risk travellers: Specific personal characteristics or complex itineraries may increase a traveller's risk of illness or require special consideration, including for travel insurance and certification to fly. Referral may be required (see Refer when section), including for (4): travellers with chronic conditions.

High risk travellers (continues from page 4): travellers with risk factors for VTE; immunocompromised travellers detailed in the CDC Yellow Book 2026: Immunocompromised travellers (3); pregnant women; young children (referral to an appropriate healthcare provider is required for all children <2 years, and may be required for other children, depending on itinerary); older people (medical practitioner assessment may be required for travel insurance purposes for adults aged ≥65 years); travellers with disabilities; travellers on extended trips; backpackers and travellers visiting friends and relatives (risks are often underestimated in these groups). Pharmacists must use their professional judgement and consider the traveller's itinerary, personal characteristics and medical history when determining the need for referral.

gates.criterion: Need for referral determined using professional judgement, the traveller's itinerary, personal characteristics and medical history

steps.description: Reminder: Pharmacists can access a range of clinical information in a patient’s My Health Record, including details about current and past medication history, allergies and current medical conditions.
Develop management plan: Pharmacists must ensure that they are prescribing medicines according to the specified sections of the current online version of the Therapeutic Guidelines.

gates.criterion: Prescribing aligns with the specified sections of the current online version of the Therapeutic Guidelines

steps.description: Vaccination: Pharmacists are responsible for confirming the specific entry and transiting vaccination requirements, risk levels and vaccine recommendations for each country and traveller. Prepare an immunisation plan for the traveller specific for their needs: Routine vaccines should be updated (if required), in addition to required and recommended travel vaccines (1, 3, 4, 6). Laboratory testing to determine immunity as a result of previous vaccination or infection may be requested for hepatitis A, hepatitis B, measles, mumps, rubella and varicella (6). Other vaccines that may be required include those used for response to a declared public health emergency, e.g., COVID-19 and monkeypox. All vaccinations must be administered in accordance with: the Australian Immunisation Handbook.

gates.criterion: Vaccination administered in accordance with the Australian Immunisation Handbook

steps.description: Vaccination (continues from page 5): the individual vaccine information provided by the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) and aligned with current Australian Technical Advisory Group on Immunisation (ATAGI) advice. Travellers who require proof of vaccination should be provided with an up-to-date International Certificate of Vaccination (ICV), commonly known as a yellow card, as outlined in Annex 6 of the WHO International Health Regulations (2005) (7). The ICV can be completed by any practitioner authorised to give vaccinations (7).

Rabies: Pre-exposure prophylaxis is recommended for people travelling to rabies-enzootic regions, based on a risk assessment; this should consider a patient's risk of rabies exposure and the patient's access to emergency medical attention in that location (refer to Table 2) (3, 6). Table 2. Risk assessment and vaccination for Rabies - Patient risk factors: Travellers who may interact with animals that could be rabid; Travellers whose occupational or recreational activities may involve contact with animals, particularly dogs; Travellers to Central and South America, Eastern Europe, Africa and Asia (the CDC conducts an annual assessment of individual countries rabies status worldwide that provides information related to rabies presence and treatment availability. See Rabies Status: Assessment by Country). Itinerary risk factors: Access to emergency medical care and post-exposure prophylaxis at the destination; Sufficient time to complete recommended pre-exposure prophylaxis prior to departure.

Rabies - Preventive measures and advice: Advise travellers, especially those with young children, to avoid contact with wild and domestic animals including stray dogs and cats. Avoid contact with bats anywhere in the world. Provide education about treatment for potential rabies exposure including first aid and requirement for post-exposure prophylaxis vaccine and, in some cases, human rabies immunoglobulin.

Rabies - Vaccination: Where pre-exposure prophylaxis is recommended, the pharmacist must prescribe the rabies vaccine in accordance with the Australian Immunisation Handbook: Rabies and other lyssaviruses and the Australian Medicines Vaccination Handbook (6, 9). The dispensed medicine may then be administered. Pre-exposure prophylaxis is recommended as a 3-dose schedule, administered on days 0, 7 and 21–28 (6, 9).

gates.criterion: Pre-exposure prophylaxis recommended on the rabies risk assessment

steps.description: Travellers' Diarrhoea: Diarrhoea is commonly experienced by travellers from industrialised countries travelling to developing countries without good sanitation; it is estimated that between 20-50% of these short-term travellers will experience diarrhoea (10). Travellers' diarrhoea can be caused by a range of pathogens, including bacterial and viral infections, depending on the location of acquisition (10). The information in Table 3 is provided as a summary only. Pharmacists should consult relevant resources to provide tailored information for each traveller. Table 3. Risk assessment and management for travellers' diarrhoea - Patient risk factors: Travellers with comorbidities such as diabetes, heart failure, bowel abnormalities, cancer, HIV or immunosuppression and older travellers are at increased risk; Young children are more likely to have severe disease; Travellers aged between 15–29 years and backpackers are at increased risk predominantly due to travel style. Itinerary risk factors: The highest risk to travellers is reported in South Asia, Sub-Saharan Africa and Latin America; Most other developing countries pose a moderate risk. Preventive measures and advice: Preventive advice for travellers: hand hygiene with soap and water or antibacterial hand wash before eating and food preparation; careful food and drink choices.

Table 3 (continued) - Preventive measures and advice: Travellers' diarrhoea is generally self-limiting and lasts between 1–3 days. Rehydration is the mainstay of therapy for travellers' diarrhoea: recognising symptoms of dehydration, appropriate fluid intake, the use of oral rehydration products, diet of light, carbohydrate-rich foods until recovered; symptoms may persist for protracted periods with pathogens that exist in chronic phase (e.g. Giardia). Early self-treatment with standby medication is preferred to antimicrobial prophylaxis for most patients due to the risk of antimicrobial resistance. Travellers at risk of severe disease who require antimicrobial prophylaxis, separate to standby treatment, must be referred to an appropriate healthcare provider.

gates.criterion: Traveller does not require antimicrobial prophylaxis, separate to standby treatment

provenance.section_heading: Table 3. Risk assessment and management for travellers' diarrhoea(3, 4, 11, 12)

steps.description: Table 3 (continued) - Pharmacotherapy (standby treatment) and supportive therapy and considerations for acute gastroenteritis: No treatment is required for mild, short episodes. Antidiarrhoeal drugs may be considered for self-treatment for adults and children >12 years (loperamide is preferred) who do not have bloody stools, systemic symptoms or fever. Most cases of travellers' diarrhoea do not require antibiotics. Self-initiated treatment with antibiotics may be acceptable for acute, moderate to severe diarrhoea only (diarrhoea that is distressing, incapacitating, interferes with or completely prevents planned activities or dysentery (bloody stools)) and reserved for those who are at increased risk of complications, and those in whom dehydration may exacerbate underlying comorbidities NB1 (12). Stand-by emergency treatment and/or standby management of associated symptoms may be provided as part of a medical kit: Antibiotics in accordance with the Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic (Infectious diarrhoea - Travellers' diarrhoea) NB1 (10). Recommended treatments include azithromycin, norfloxacin and ciprofloxacin as single-dose therapy. Antidiarrhoeal drugs in accordance with the Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal (Acute gastroenteritis – Other supportive therapy and considerations for acute gastroenteritis - Antidiarrhoeal drugs for acute gastroenteritis) (11). NB1: The benefits of antibiotic therapy for travellers' diarrhoea must be weighed against the risks of adverse effects. Antibiotic use may lead to acquisition of resistant organisms that may cause urinary tract infection, Clostridioides difficile infection, and post-travel irritable bowel syndrome. Emerging resistance to quinolones, particularly in South Asia, should be considered.

gates.criterion: Adult or child >12 years without bloody stools, systemic symptoms or fever (antidiarrhoeal self-treatment)
Antibiotic therapy clinically indicated for acute, moderate to severe diarrhoea

provenance.section_heading: Table 3. Risk assessment and management for travellers' diarrhoea(3, 4, 11, 12)

steps.description: Table 3 - Post travel: Persistent diarrhoea (>2 weeks duration) in returned travellers may have infective or non-infective causes and must be referred to an appropriate healthcare provider for investigation.

gates.criterion: Persistent diarrhoea (>2 weeks duration) in a returned traveller

provenance.section_heading: Table 3. Risk assessment and management for travellers' diarrhoea(3, 4, 11, 12)

steps.description: Reminder: The prescribing and use of antibiotics should be consistent with the principles described in the Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic. Pharmacists should carefully assess whether antibiotic therapy is clinically indicated, and if so, consider local antimicrobial resistance patterns and relevant clinical factors when selecting therapy.

gates.criterion: Antibiotic therapy clinically indicated (assessed against Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic principles)

steps.description: Malaria: In humans, malaria is caused by one of five species of Plasmodium parasites, most often transmitted through the bite of an infected mosquito, although transmission occasionally occurs through needle sharing, nosocomially or from mother to foetus (3, 4, 13). Illness usually occurs within a few weeks of the infection, although it may be delayed by several months (4, 13). Almost all cases of malaria in Australia are overseas acquired. However, parts of Northern Australia are malaria-receptive; the last local acquired case was reported in the Torres Strait Islands in 2013 (4). The risk of malaria can vary considerably between travellers and regions within the same country (3). Modifiable risk factors associated with malaria fatalities include inappropriate use (or no use) of chemoprophylaxis and delay in seeking care (diagnosis and treatment) (4). Table 4 is provided as a summary only. Table 4. Risk assessment, management and prophylaxis for malaria - Patient risk factors: Travellers at risk of severe disease must be referred to an appropriate healthcare provider. Itinerary/destination risk factors: For Australian travellers, the most common destinations of acquisition are India and Papua New Guinea, followed by Africa (4); Travellers visiting friends and relatives in endemic countries (risk may be underappreciated by these travellers); Travel in malaria endemic areas for longer than 8 weeks. Preventive measures and advice: All travellers to countries where malaria is endemic should be provided with advice on mosquito avoidance and the risks of malaria, including: prevention through use of effective insect repellent, other insecticide products and mosquito nets, remaining indoors from dusk to dawn where possible, wearing long trousers and long-sleeved shirts in the evening and avoiding strong fragrances; no chemoprophylaxis regimen is guaranteed to be 100% effective. Emergency treatment must be sought for febrile illness (even if stand-by treatment has been taken); treatment for malaria may be available without a prescription overseas. However, counterfeit products are common.

Table 4 - Pharmacotherapy (prophylactic and standby emergency treatment of uncomplicated malaria): To determine whether chemoprophylaxis is required and the appropriate medicines to provide, pharmacists should consider: (the list of considerations continues on page 10 - see next step).

provenance.section_heading: Table 4. Risk assessment, management and prophylaxis for malaria (3, 4, 13)

steps.description: Table 4 - Pharmacotherapy (continues from page 9): destination(s), including regions and seasons within endemic countries and current government recommendations including patterns of antimalarial resistance in the destination(s); the individual's risk of mosquito bites; the individual's risk of severe malarial illness; the individual's risk of adverse effects and drug toxicity, and ability to swallow the prescribed prophylaxis; the individual's other medical conditions, allergy history, other medications; the potential for resistance to chemoprophylactic drugs; the cost and efficacy of each drug (3, 4, 13). If required, antimalarial chemoprophylaxis may be prescribed in accordance with the Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic (Parasitic infections – Malaria) (13). Stand-by emergency treatment should be prescribed to people travelling to malaria-endemic areas who choose not to use chemoprophylaxis as part of a medical kit (for when emergency medical care cannot be obtained within 24 hours) in accordance with the Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic (Parasitic infections – Malaria) (13).

gates.criterion: Traveller not within the 'Refer when' criteria for malaria prophylaxis or stand-by treatment (children aged ≤8 years ... or who require malaria prophylaxis or stand-by treatment; areas where malaria is endemic for longer than 8 weeks; pregnant travellers or travellers planning to become pregnant while travelling)

provenance.section_heading: Table 4. Risk assessment, management and prophylaxis for malaria (3, 4, 13)

steps.description: Table 4 - Post travel: All people who fall ill during or after travel and have persisting symptoms should be referred to an appropriate healthcare provider.

provenance.section_heading: Table 4. Risk assessment, management and prophylaxis for malaria (3, 4, 13)

steps.description: Reminder (repeats the page 8 reminder): The prescribing and use of antibiotics should be consistent with the principles described in the Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic. Pharmacists should carefully assess whether antibiotic therapy is clinically indicated, and if so, consider local antimicrobial resistance patterns and relevant clinical factors when selecting therapy.

High altitude travel and altitude illness: Altitude is assumed to start at 1,200 m. Elevations above 1,500 m are considered high altitude (14). While the highest risk of altitude illness is in environments >2,500 m above sea-level, it may also occur at altitudes from 1,500 m. Normal physiological changes due to hypobaric hypoxia will occur in all people at high altitudes, including shortness of breath on exertion (normal if it resolves quickly on rest), increased urination, disturbed sleep with periods of hyperpnoea and dyspnoea at night (4). Altitude illness describes a set of pathological syndromes that may be experienced when a person ascends to a high altitude environment too quickly without allowing for sufficient time to acclimatise (14, 15).

provenance.section_heading: High altitude travel and altitude illness

steps.description: Altitude illness syndromes: Acute mountain sickness (AMS) (most common type) is characterised by a headache and at least one of gastrointestinal symptoms, fatigue or weakness, or dizziness/light-headedness. High-altitude cerebral oedema (HACE) (usually a progression of AMS but not always) is rare below 4300 m. It is a medical emergency and requires immediate descent (3, 14). High-altitude pulmonary oedema (HAPE) may occur on its own or with AMS and HACE. It is a medical emergency and requires immediate descent (3, 14). The information in Table 5 is provided as a summary only. Pharmacists should consult relevant resources to provide tailored information for each traveller.

provenance.section_heading: High altitude travel and altitude illness

steps.description: Table 5. Risk assessment, prevention and management of altitude sickness - Patient risk factors: There can be significant variation in how individuals with pre-existing conditions may react to exposure to high altitude. Travellers with the following pre-existing medical conditions may be at increased risk of altitude illness and must be referred to an appropriate healthcare provider: cardiovascular disorders (hypertension, coronary artery disease, heart failure, cardiac arrhythmias, congenital heart disease, recent myocardial infarction or stroke); Raynaud’s Phenomenon; chronic kidney disease; cirrhosis; coagulopathy and people taking warfarin; cystic fibrosis; damage to carotid bodies; diabetes; gastrointestinal conditions (active peptic ulcer, active inflammatory bowel disease); haematological conditions (iron deficiency anaemia, sickle cell disease); neurological disorders (epilepsy, cerebrovascular disease, migraine); obesity; ophthalmic conditions (radial keratotomy, LASIK); pregnancy; respiratory disorders (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, bronchial asthma, obstructive sleep apnoea, pulmonary hypertension, pleural and interstitial lung disease); psychiatric conditions.

gates.criterion: Traveller has none of the pre-existing medical conditions listed as increasing risk of altitude illness

provenance.section_heading: Table 5. Risk assessment, prevention and management of altitude sickness (3, 4, 14, 15, 16)

steps.description: Table 5 (continued) - Patient risk factors: The symptoms of altitude illness may impact other existing medical conditions (cough, disturbed sleep, cold related illnesses, photokeratitis, corneal thickening and retinal haemorrhages). Children do not appear to be at higher risk of altitude illness, however, there is limited evidence for specific recommendations (14).

provenance.section_heading: Table 5. Risk assessment, prevention and management of altitude sickness (3, 4, 14, 15, 16)

steps.description: Table 5 (continued) - Referral criteria and environmental risk: Children aged <8 years travelling to elevations >2,500 m should be referred to a suitable healthcare provider for specialist advice. Travellers with any of the above pre-existing medical conditions planning to travel to high altitudes (>1,500 m) must be referred to a suitable healthcare provider for specialist advice and detailed risk assessment. Environmental factors that influence the risk of altitude illness include: the speed and maximum height of ascent (risk of ascent); sleeping elevation; strenuous exertion at altitude e.g., skiing or trekking (15, 17). Altitude illness is a risk in a range of common destinations for multiple kinds of travellers, including: tourists with relatively common itineraries with elevations above >2,500 m above sea-level; consider the potential for rapid passive ascent to high altitudes (driving, train travel, flying, hot-air ballooning, cable cars and ski lifts etc); people who live below 900 m and engage in strenuous exertion or activities on arrival in high altitude areas e.g., trekking or skiing.

gates.criterion: Traveller is aged ≥8 years and has none of the pre-existing medical conditions listed as requiring referral for high-altitude travel

provenance.section_heading: Table 5. Risk assessment, prevention and management of altitude sickness (3, 4, 14, 15, 16)

steps.description: Low, medium and high-risk ascents for AMS (for unacclimatised individuals) (14, 17). Low risk: no history of AMS when ascending to ≤2,800 m; ascents taking ≥2 days to reach 2,500 m–3,000 m, with further increases in sleeping elevation to a maximum of 500 m per day and an extra day for acclimatisation for every 1,000 m of ascent. Moderate risk: no history of AMS when ascending to >2800 m in one day; history of AMS when ascending to 2,500 m–2,800 m in one day; increases in sleeping elevation >500 m per day and when above 3,000 m with an extra day for acclimatisation every 1,000 m. High risk: history of AMS when ascending to >2800 m in one day; history of HAPE or HACE (at any altitude); ascents to elevations >3,500 m in one day; increases in sleeping elevation >500 m per day when above 3,000 m without extra days for acclimatisation; very rapid ascent e.g., ascent to areas of extreme altitude (>5,800 m) in <7 days.

provenance.section_heading: Low, medium and high-risk ascents for AMS (for unacclimatised individuals) (14, 17)

steps.description: Travellers with a history of altitude illness or at moderate or high risk of AMS must be referred to an appropriate healthcare provider for management.

gates.criterion: Traveller has no history of altitude illness and is assessed at low risk of AMS

provenance.section_heading: High altitude travel and altitude illness

steps.description: Preventive measures and advice: There is no guarantee of the absolute effectiveness of any preventative strategies; vigilance is required. All people planning to travel to elevations above 2,500 m should plan for a gradual, low risk ascent to enable acclimatisation and prevent altitude illness, specifically: take at least 2 days to ascend to 3,000 m; do not increase sleeping altitude by more than 500 m per day if above 3,000 m; allow an extra day for acclimatisation every 1,000 m of sleeping altitude gain. If gradual ascent is not possible (e.g., flying into a high-altitude airport), take extra rest days before and after.

provenance.section_heading: High altitude travel and altitude illness

steps.description: Preventive measures and advice (continued): Advice should also be provided to the traveller regarding: the importance of appropriate travel insurance; physical fitness, an appropriate medical kit, clothing and eye wear; travelling/trekking with an experienced guide at high altitudes; how to recognise the signs of altitude illness (AMS, HACE and HAPE) and that it can be potentially fatal, specifically: all symptoms at high altitude should be considered altitude sickness until determined otherwise; seek medical care as soon as signs or symptoms are experienced; never ascend to a higher altitude to sleep with symptoms of altitude sickness; do not leave a person with suspected altitude illness alone; always attempt to descend if symptoms are severe or worsen; other conditions that may be experienced at altitude including sun exposure, hypothermia and cold injury.

provenance.section_heading: High altitude travel and altitude illness

steps.description: Pharmacotherapy (standby): Travellers at low risk of altitude illness generally do not require pharmacological prophylaxis. General treatment for altitude illness includes stopping, resting and rehydrating; the most effective treatment is descent. Oral standby treatment may be prescribed for adults for the initial management of altitude illness as part of a medical kit (with appropriate instructions for use in the event the person cannot seek immediate medical care or descend) to people at low risk of altitude illness travelling to elevations >2,500 m in accordance with the Therapeutic Guidelines: Wilderness Medicine (Altitude illness) (15).

gates.criterion: Adult traveller assessed at low risk of altitude illness travelling to elevations >2,500 m

provenance.section_heading: High altitude travel and altitude illness

steps.description: Pharmacotherapy (standby) (sentence continues on page 14): Oral standby treatment may be prescribed for management of nausea and vomiting associated with altitude sickness for patients who cannot seek immediate medical care and/or descend, in accordance with the Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal (Nausea and Vomiting) (18).

gates.criterion: Patient cannot seek immediate medical care and/or descend

provenance.section_heading: High altitude travel and altitude illness

steps.description: Venous Thromboembolism (VTE): Venous thromboembolism is a rare, but serious, complication of long-distance travel. The information in Table 6 is provided as a summary only. Pharmacists should consult relevant resources to provide tailored information for each traveller. Table 6 - Patient risk factors: In addition to long-distance travel, risk factors for VTE (that may indicate the need for pharmacologic prophylaxis) include: previous history of VTE; reduced mobility (at least 3 days); older age (≥60 years); medical conditions including thrombophilia, rheumatological disorders, active malignancies, or heart or respiratory failure; chemotherapy or radiotherapy within the previous 6 months; recent trauma/surgery (within previous month); obesity; pregnancy and postpartum period; ongoing hormonal treatment (4, 21). Travellers with one or more additional risk factors for VTE (as above) should have their risk estimated using a VTE risk calculator, such as the Padua Prediction Score for Risk of VTE and be referred to an appropriate healthcare provider if VTE prophylaxis is indicated.

gates.criterion: No additional VTE risk factors (as above), or VTE prophylaxis not indicated after risk estimation using a VTE risk calculator

provenance.section_heading: Table 6. Risk assessment, prevention and management of VTE (3, 4, 19–21)

steps.description: Table 6 - Patient risk factors (continued): Patients at moderate to high risk of VTE must be referred to a specialised travel medicine clinic or their treating medical practitioner for specialist advice and detailed risk assessment.

gates.criterion: Patient not at moderate to high risk of VTE

provenance.section_heading: Table 6. Risk assessment, prevention and management of VTE (3, 4, 19–21)

steps.description: Table 6 - Itinerary and environmental risk factors: Long-distance travel (travel by air, road or rail of 4 hours duration or greater) has been associated with VTE, particularly air travel ≥8 hours, although the absolute risk is low (21). The risk of VTE may remain for up to 8 weeks post travel (21).

provenance.section_heading: Table 6. Risk assessment, prevention and management of VTE (3, 4, 19–21)

steps.description: Table 6 - Preventive measures and advice: General advice to minimise the risk of VTE for all long-distance travellers includes: remaining ambulant before and after travel; regular movement during travel such as thigh and calf stretching and exercises; ensuring there is adequate legroom wherever possible (by sitting in an aisle seat or emergency exit seat); avoiding alcohol and sedatives before and during travel; wearing loose clothing (4, 6) (final item printed on page 15).

provenance.section_heading: Table 6. Risk assessment, prevention and management of VTE (3, 4, 19–21)

steps.description: Table 6 (continued) - Preventive measures and advice: The use of graduated compression stockings is not routinely recommended for travellers at low risk of VTE, however they may reduce asymptomatic deep vein thrombosis and assist with preventing leg swelling (6). All compression stockings should be professionally fitted (6).

steps.description: Medical Kits: Medical kits should be considered by all travellers, including those visiting low risk destinations (4). The contents should be tailored to each traveller based on destination and patient-specific factors (4). The contents of a medical kit should be documented and include written instructions for use. Things that should be considered for each traveller when compiling a medical kit include: documentation: immunisation record; documentation of pre-existing conditions; copies of prescriptions and letter from the pharmacist for travelling with medications, including stand-by medications; travel insurance details; basic first aid kit; common over-the-counter medications: analgesics; antacids; antidiarrhoeals; antiemetics and medication for motion sickness; antifungal cream; antihistamines; antispasmodics; cough suppressant or expectorant; decongestants (consider regulations in destination); laxatives (list continues on page 16); hydrocortisone cream; rehydration products; standby treatments for malaria, diarrhoea and altitude sickness (as appropriate) with instructions for use; usual medications and medical equipment; other preventative items, for example: contraception; condoms; insect repellents and bed netting; water purification tablets; hand sanitiser and/or wipes; face masks; sunscreen; medical alert bracelet or other identifiers; spare glasses or contact lenses.

Travelling with medications: People planning to take any type of medication or supplements overseas (including prescribed and non-prescribed medicines and medical equipment), particularly controlled substances, must confirm any restrictions and requirements/permits with the destination country’s embassy or consulate. All medicines should be carried in their original packaging, clearly labelled with the contents, patient name and dose; travellers should be advised not to use pillboxes (3). Travellers may also consider carrying copies of their prescriptions and a letter from the prescriber detailing all medicines they have been prescribed, the reasons they have been prescribed, doses, and any necessary medical equipment including syringes. Translated versions may also assist (3). Medications should be packed in carry-on luggage and an extra supply should be included in the event the trip is extended (3).

gates.criterion: Restrictions and requirements/permits confirmed with the destination country’s embassy or consulate

steps.description: Provide travel health education and counselling: Comprehensive advice and counselling (including supporting written information when required) should be provided to the patient regarding: individual product and medicine use, including dosing and indications; non-pharmacological management; how to manage adverse effects; accessing medications, treatment and health advice; seeking medical care and/or treatment post travel for ongoing issues (final bullet printed on page 17).

provenance.section_heading: Provide travel health education and counselling

steps.description: Provide travel health education and counselling (continues from page 16): Travellers should be counselled and provided with advice to enable safe travel and risk minimisation (4). The topics and level of detail will vary between travellers, depending on the personal and itinerary risks identified during the pre-travel risk assessment (2). Travellers should be advised to sign up for Smartraveller subscriber alerts for up-to-date information about health risks. Common issues to be discussed for all travellers may include (2, 4): emerging health issues and diseases relevant to the traveller; appropriate travel insurance; personal safety. Other topics (as applicable) (4): choosing safe food and drinks; insect and other pest avoidance; avoiding environmental exposures (contaminated soil and water); dog or other animal bite management; injuries including aquatic and traffic accidents; alcohol and drug use; weather conditions and potential for natural disasters; prevention of VTE; availability of counterfeit medications or supplements; safe sex practices; blood borne infections (acquired through cosmetic/medical procedures, tattoos, piercings and intravenous drug use); altitude illness and the importance of planned gradual ascent; staying safe in conflicts or situations of civil unrest; motion sickness; international driving licences. It is the pharmacist’s responsibility to ensure the suitability and accuracy of any resources provided to patients, and to ensure compliance with all copyright conditions.

steps.description: Clinical Review: Clinical review with the pharmacist post travel is not required. Patients should be instructed as to any required follow-up vaccination doses. All patients should be advised during the pre-travel consultation to see their usual healthcare provider as soon as they return if they have health issues post-travel.

treatments.notes: Pre-exposure prophylaxis is recommended for people travelling to rabies-enzootic regions, based on a risk assessment (considering risk of rabies exposure and access to emergency medical attention) (3, 6). Where recommended, the pharmacist must prescribe the rabies vaccine in accordance with the Australian Immunisation Handbook: Rabies and other lyssaviruses and the Australian Medicines Vaccination Handbook (6, 9); the dispensed medicine may then be administered. Pre-exposure prophylaxis is recommended as a 3-dose schedule, administered on days 0, 7 and 21–28 (6, 9). No vaccine strength, volume, route or maximum dose is printed in this document.

Rehydration is the mainstay of therapy for travellers' diarrhoea: recognising symptoms of dehydration, appropriate fluid intake, the use of oral rehydration products, diet of light, carbohydrate-rich foods until recovered (3, 4, 11, 12). Travellers' diarrhoea is generally self-limiting and lasts between 1–3 days. No strength, sachet quantity or frequency is printed in this document.

treatments.notes: No treatment is required for mild, short episodes. Prescribe in accordance with the Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal (Acute gastroenteritis – Other supportive therapy and considerations for acute gastroenteritis - Antidiarrhoeal drugs for acute gastroenteritis) (11). treatments.notes: Stand-by emergency treatment and/or standby management of associated symptoms may be provided as part of a medical kit: antibiotics in accordance with the Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic (Infectious diarrhoea - Travellers' diarrhoea) NB1 (10). Recommended treatments include azithromycin, norfloxacin and ciprofloxacin as single-dose therapy. NB1: The benefits of antibiotic therapy for travellers' diarrhoea must be weighed against the risks of adverse effects; antibiotic use may lead to acquisition of resistant organisms that may cause urinary tract infection, Clostridioides difficile infection, and post-travel irritable bowel syndrome. Most cases of travellers' diarrhoea do not require antibiotics; self-initiated antibiotic treatment is for acute, moderate to severe diarrhoea only. No mg dose is printed in this document.

treatments.drug: Antimalarial chemoprophylaxis (Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic (Parasitic infections – Malaria))
treatments.notes: If required, antimalarial chemoprophylaxis may be prescribed in accordance with the Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic (Parasitic infections – Malaria) (13). To determine whether chemoprophylaxis is required and the appropriate medicines, consider: destination(s), including regions and seasons within endemic countries and current government recommendations including patterns of antimalarial resistance; the individual's risk of mosquito bites; risk of severe malarial illness; risk of adverse effects and drug toxicity, and ability to swallow the prescribed prophylaxis; other medical conditions, allergy history, other medications; potential for resistance to chemoprophylactic drugs; cost and efficacy of each drug (3, 4, 13). No chemoprophylaxis regimen is guaranteed to be 100% effective. No specific drug name, strength, dose, route or frequency is printed in this document; commencement ideally 6-8 weeks before departure.

treatments.notes: Oral standby treatment may be prescribed for adults for the initial management of altitude illness as part of a medical kit (with appropriate instructions for use in the event the person cannot seek immediate medical care or descend) to people at low risk of altitude illness travelling to elevations >2,500 m in accordance with the Therapeutic Guidelines: Wilderness Medicine (Altitude illness) (15). Travellers at low risk of altitude illness generally do not require pharmacological prophylaxis. General treatment for altitude illness includes stopping, resting and rehydrating; the most effective treatment is descent. No drug name, strength or dose is printed in this document.
